issues.detail: Covers the happy path and a few log or default-file checks, but gives little troubleshooting for failures such as GPU/Vulkan problems on Linux, an unreachable Ollama server, or a formatter that cannot be found.

scenarios.name: typescript-prettier-vim-settings
scenarios.rationale: A fully meets the rubric with vim_mode, format_on_save "on", external prettier formatters for TypeScript and TSX using --stdin-filepath and {buffer_path}, and it names both ~/.config/zed/settings.json and the `zed: open settings file` command, while B has the same snippet content but names neither of those, giving only keyboard shortcuts and `zed: open settings`, and adds a redundant global formatter plus unrequested languages.

scenarios.name: ollama-agent-no-secret-predictions
scenarios.rationale: A covers every rubric item (pull and serve, api_url, context_window 16384, edit_predictions.disabled_globs for .env/.pem/.key, no API key), whereas B has no context_window and only a vague note about max_tokens and num_ctx, and it also adds speculative settings (tool_permissions, features) it admits are from memory.

scenarios.name: write-gleam-lsp-extension
scenarios.rationale: Both give the correct top-level extension.toml with languages = ["Gleam"], zed::Extension with worktree.which("gleam") and args ["lsp"], register_extension!, and cdylib. B states outright that there is no [extension] table, and it covers `zed: install dev extension`, `zed: open log` and `zed --foreground`. A has the same testing coverage plus useful extras, but it puts zed_extension_api in Cargo.toml with an uncertain pinned version and adds a `name` field to the language server section. B leaves the crate dependency to `cargo add zed_extension_api`, so the dependency isn't shown in Cargo.toml itself, which is a small gap against the rubric.
